source.title: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreak Attacks via In-Decoding Safety-Awareness Probing
source.authors: Yinzhi Zhao; Ming Wang; Shi Feng; Xiaocui Yang; Da-Ling Wang; Yi-Fei Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites shallow safety alignment as motivation and uses probing of latent safety signals to build a jailbreak defense. Its reported defense results do not test the claim versions about alignment fine-tuning, per-token KL, bypassing the opening, safety localization, causes of shallowness, or deepening safety.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SafeProbing defense success rates, over-refusal counts, capability scores, and probing-ratio comparisons. These are results of its own detection defense, not measurements of the claim versions; the defense is deliberately induced and therefore its performance is not evidence that the underlying models otherwise exhibit the claimed behavior. The paper cites the original studies but does not reproduce their methods. Table 5's clause comparison is used to select the disclaimer clause. Table 8 concerns multimodal transfer of the detector, not a claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites shallow alignment (Qi et al. 2025) as motivation and builds a decoding-time disclaimer-loss detector. Its reported results are defense success rates, over-refusal counts and utility of its own method. It does not measure per-token KL, run fine-tuning attacks, localize safety weights, or train deeper alignment. The no-defense baselines show that prompt-based jailbreaks (AutoDAN, PAIR, ReNeLLM, DRA, etc.) succeed. These are input-side attacks on AdvBench, not tests of prefilled openings, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes. The study does not attribute the bypass to the opening tokens, so it does not test V4 either.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that LLMs retain latent safety-awareness while generating harmful content. Probing it during decoding with a disclaimer-loss signal, plus light LoRA enhancement, gives an effective jailbreak defense with low over-refusal and preserved utility.
record.recipe_differences: This is a decoding-time disclaimer-loss detector with lightweight LoRA training and refusal intervention, not a replication of either original study's fine-tuning or per-token KL measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that probing during decoding separates harmful and benign disclaimer-loss distributions better than checking only after completion; it also varies the decoding-check ratio, threshold, disclaimer clause, and training hyperparameter.

fits_no_version.finding: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, mean disclaimer-core loss is lower on harmful than benign samples (in-decoding 0.58 vs 5.58; last-check 3.07 vs 8.34). Separation is larger when probed during decoding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A disclaimer-loss probe separates harmful from benign outputs more clearly during decoding than after the full response.

fits_no_version.finding: Jailbroken models sometimes append disclaimers after harmful content. Probe loss drops right after harmful spans appear mid-response (Fig. 4, Appendix C). This suggests a latent recognition of harm deep into the response that does not trigger refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: After safety is bypassed, aligned models still encode recognition of harmfulness at later response positions, but it does not trigger self-correction.

record.problems: The reported claim-related probe comparison is for one model and its stated means; uncertainty estimates are not reported for these values. The paper does not directly measure any of the seven claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version results were available to extract. SafeProbing defense rates and other defense-performance results in Tables 1–4 and 6 are outcomes of the paper's own induced detection defense, rather than tests of the claim versions. Table 5's clause values are used to select a probe clause; Table 8 reports detector signals under multimodal inputs, outside the listed versions.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples; the LoRA training is for the detector, and harmful compliance is not measured.
No test of benign fine-tuning raising harmful compliance.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL by response position.
No prefilling, GCG-style suffix or decoding-change attacks. Prompt-based jailbreak success appears only as a no-defense baseline and is not linked to the opening tokens.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks.
No test of data or objective as the cause of shallowness.
No training that spreads refusal across response positions; SafeProbing is an external detector with hard refusal.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T4/uses_without_test classification stands. Rows R1–R4 are correctly linked to none with state cannot_determine: they are detector signals, not a claim behaviour. The no-defense DSRs in Tables 1 and 6 (e.g., Qwen AutoDAN 14.0%, DRA 5.6%) show that jailbreak prompts succeed. They do not isolate the opening-token mechanism V4 names, so they are not recorded as V4 rows. The latent-awareness observation is conceptually adjacent to shallow alignment, since harm recognition persists past the first tokens without producing refusal. It is not a measured test of any listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune models on harmful examples to measure harmful-request compliance.
Does not test whether ordinary or selected benign fine-tuning raises harmful compliance.
Does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL across response positions.
Does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as the claimed bypass mechanisms.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Does not test whether training data or objective causes safety shallowness.
Does not test training that spreads safety beyond early response tokens or whether such training holds up.
